# Gartner, Inc. (NYSE: IT) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Five consecutive quarterly calls, May 2025 through May 2026, cross-checked against the reported financials, the price tape, and the litigation record. Price used throughout: $150.41 (NYSE, US dollars, live quote 27 July 2026). Gartner sells subscription research and advice to senior executives; its single most important operating number is contract value, the annualised dollar amount of research subscriptions on its books at a point in time.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across five calls the story does not change its facts so much as it steadily relocates the finish line.

**May 2025 (first quarter 2025).** The tone is one of confident endurance. Contract value grew 7%. Gene Hall, the chairman and chief executive, frames a hard environment as temporary and enumerates the shocks the company has already survived — "the COVID-19 pandemic, the bursting of a tech spending bubble, the highest inflation in 40 years." The forward promise is specific and quantified: "We expect to reaccelerate CV growth to our target of 12% to 16%, when the macroeconomic environment returns to normal." Blame is assigned to two identifiable, containable buckets: the US federal government (about 4% of contract value, hit by the Department of Government Efficiency) and tariffs.

**August 2025 (second quarter).** The narrative pivots hard, and this is the most important shift in the whole sequence. Hall opens by naming two takeaways, and the first is artificial intelligence: "AI is an important opportunity for Gartner across several dimensions." The second is an admission dressed as a plan — "we're making adaptations that give us a clear path back to double-digit growth." Note the quiet demotion: in May the target was 12–16%; by August the aspiration is "double-digit." The company also renames its largest segment from Research to Business and Technology Insights, and launches AskGartner, an artificial-intelligence assistant that has "been in development for almost 2 years." A new headwind is introduced: "Measures of CEO confidence fell to recessionary levels, among the fastest drops ever recorded."

**November 2025 (third quarter).** Contract value growth is 3%, less than half the level of two quarters earlier. The emphasis moves decisively from growth to proof-of-engagement metrics and to capital returns: "we repurchased more than $1 billion of stock in the quarter, reducing share count by 6% year-over-year." The reacceleration language softens again, now qualified by time: a "clear path back to long-term sustained double-digit growth **over the medium term**."

**February 2026 (fourth quarter).** This is the capitulation call, and the market treated it as one — the stock fell 31% in a single session. Hall abandons the "the environment will normalise" frame entirely and replaces it with a structural self-criticism: "driving incremental improvements on our standard practices wasn't enough. To achieve step change improvements, we needed to rethink many of our processes and practices." The transformation is formalised along four dimensions — impact, volume, timeliness, user experience. Crucially, the payoff window is pushed out again: "We believe this transformation will provide a step change in the value to our clients **over the next few years**." A definitive agreement to sell the Digital Markets business is disclosed alongside.

**May 2026 (first quarter 2026).** A modest, genuine stabilisation. Contract value grew 1% — an acceleration, from a very low base. Free cash flow rose 29% year over year. Guidance for profit, earnings and cash flow was raised. And the growth promise is restated one more time, in yet another new form: "we expect to deliver adjusted EPS on a compound annual basis above 12% over the next 3 years." Observe what has happened over five calls: the 12–16% *contract value* target of May 2025 has become a 12% *earnings per share* target — and earnings per share is the one line a large buyback can deliver regardless of what the business does.

**Quietly dropped along the way:** the phrase "return to historically strong productivity"; the specific 12–16% contract-value target; and the framing that the headwinds are federal-government and tariff-specific. **Quietly added:** artificial intelligence as both the top client demand topic and the company's own product story; share-count reduction as the headline shareholder-value mechanism.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where and when | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We expect to reaccelerate CV growth to our target of 12% to 16%" | Hall, Q1 2025 | Contract value growth went 7% (Q1 2025) → 3% (Q3 2025) → 0.8% (Q4 2025) → 1% (Q1 2026). The target was never approached; it was silently replaced. | **Contradicted** |
| "a clear path back to double-digit growth" | Hall, Q2 2025 | Repeated in some form on every subsequent call. Two quarters after it was first said, growth hit 0.8%. Consensus revenue for 2026 is $6.43B against $6.50B delivered in 2025 — a *decline*. | **Contradicted** |
| Financial results "ahead of expectations" | Every one of the five calls | True, and consistently so. Reported earnings per share beat the consensus estimate in all seven of the last seven quarters: $2.50 vs $2.37, $2.98 vs $2.72, $3.53 vs $3.30, $2.76 vs $2.43, $3.94 vs $3.50, $3.32 vs $2.99. | **Corroborated** |
| Margins and cash generation are holding | Safian, Q3 2025 and Q1 2026 | Genuinely strong. Total contribution margin (revenue less the direct cost of delivering it) rose from 69% in Q3 2025 to 72% in Q1 2026. Gross margin is a stable 67.7%. First-quarter 2026 free cash flow was $371M, up 29%. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $1.26B on $6.5B of revenue — an 18% free-cash-flow margin. | **Corroborated** |
| "we generate free cash flow well in excess of net income" | Hall, repeatedly | Correct and materially so: $1.26B of trailing free cash flow against roughly $741M of trailing net income, a ratio of about 1.7x, because subscriptions are billed in advance. | **Corroborated** |
| Pricing power is intact; "we do not offer discounts" | Safian, Q1 2026; Hall, Q3 2025 on the 3.5% list increase | Supported by the margin evidence above and by rising wallet retention. Also supported by a fact outside the filings: in the eight weeks to 27 July 2026 at least fifteen separate technology vendors issued press releases advertising their placement in a Gartner Magic Quadrant. Vendors do not pay to publicise a badge that has stopped mattering. | **Corroborated** |
| Buybacks are executed "by being price sensitive, opportunistic, and disciplined" | Hall, Q1 2025 | This is the single worst-supported claim in the file. See below. | **Contradicted, severely** |

### The buyback, priced against the tape

Gartner repurchased about $2.0 billion of its own stock during 2025 (cash-flow statement: $163M, $274M, $1,056M and $498M by quarter) and a further $535M in the first quarter of 2026 — roughly $2.5 billion in five quarters, equal to about a quarter of today's entire $10.1 billion market value.

The largest single tranche, $1.056 billion, was spent in the quarter ended September 2025. Gartner shares closed at $352.47 on 28 July 2025, $336.71 on 4 August 2025, and traded between roughly $226 and $265 for the balance of that quarter. A reasonable average execution price for that tranche is around $250. The stock is $150.41 today. That one quarter's repurchase is worth roughly 40% less than what was paid for it — on the order of $400 million of value transferred from continuing holders to exiting ones.

It gets harder to defend. On the February 2026 call Hall listed among 2025's "shareholder value-enhancing actions" both the $2 billion of buybacks and "increasing leverage with a successful inaugural investment-grade bond offering to support even more share repurchase capacity." The cash-flow statement confirms $525M of net debt issuance in the fourth quarter of 2025. Gartner borrowed money to buy its own shares at roughly $250 while telling investors the programme was price-sensitive. Net debt now stands at $1.69 billion (borrowings of $2.98B plus $372M of capitalised leases, less $1.67B of cash) against a balance sheet whose book equity has been reduced to $63 million.

To be fair to the other side of the ledger: at today's $150 the same programme is genuinely powerful. Trailing free cash flow of $1.26 billion against a $10.1 billion market value means Gartner can retire something like a tenth of its own shares every year without borrowing a dollar. The criticism is of the execution, not the instrument.

### The gap between reported and adjusted profit

In the quarter ended September 2025, Gartner reported adjusted earnings of $2.76 per share. Reported earnings under standard accounting rules were $0.47 per share — a factor of nearly six. The cash-flow statement shows a $256 million non-cash item added back that quarter, and reported operating income collapsed to $86 million from a roughly $330 million quarterly run-rate. That single quarter is the arithmetic reason the full-year 2025 earnings per share of $9.65 was down 40% year over year while every quarterly press release said results were "ahead of expectations." Investors reading only the adjusted line would not have registered it.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: declining, then stabilising at a lower level.**

- *Q1 2025 — offensive.* "We'll target our investments to support long-term sustained double-digit growth." Headcount in sales grew 4%. The company is investing into the downturn.
- *Q2 2025 — first defensive turn.* The vocabulary changes to adaptation and containment: "we're making adaptations," "we're expanding our capabilities," and, on costs, "we're prepared to tighten the belt maybe one more notch if we have to." Safian confirms sales headcount will "end the year roughly flattish."
- *Q3 2025 — proof-seeking.* Growth metrics are replaced by leading indicators of growth: "Client engagement was up in the quarter," "our new business pipeline is up double digits," "Attendee ratings of our conferences are reaching all-time highs." When a company substitutes engagement statistics for revenue statistics, it is telling you the revenue statistics are not ready.
- *Q4 2025 — defensive and self-critical.* "Executives have responded to this by slowing and deferring everything possible. This makes for a much tougher selling environment." Then the striking planning assumption from the analyst session: "we're certainly assuming that this year 2026, that the selling environment is going to be no better anticipated in 2025... we're assuming behind is not going to get better at all." That is prudent, and it is also the first time in the sequence that management has stopped forecasting a recovery in demand.
- *Q1 2026 — cautiously constructive.* "New business with enterprise leaders was strong in the first 2 months of the quarter. Due to changes in the geopolitical environment, client decisions slowed somewhat in March." Note the precision — they are now dating the slowdown to a specific month, which is a more falsifiable and therefore more credible form of disclosure than the sweeping macro narratives of a year earlier.

On specificity, the record actually improves. Early calls offered a sweeping numeric target with no delivery. Recent calls offer narrower, checkable claims — "the number of high-impact documents [is up] 22%," "the number of documents in our insights library is up 19%," "we've reduced our average publishing time by 75% compared to last year," "licensed users who use AskGartner had substantially higher renewal rates than those who did not even with the same levels of engagement." These are testable. Management has traded the grand promise for the modest measurable, which is usually what a management team does when it has been burned — and it is a mild positive for credibility going forward.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: low-to-medium.** The split is unusually clean and worth stating precisely, because the two halves point in opposite directions.

**What they have delivered, without exception: profit, margin and cash.** Seven consecutive quarterly earnings beats. Guidance for profit, earnings and free cash flow was *raised* in both November 2025 and May 2026, in the middle of the worst demand stretch in a decade. Free cash flow of $1.26 billion over the last twelve months exceeds net income by about 70%. Management controls costs with real skill — Safian's description of "territory optimization," reallocating sales coverage away from the shrinking federal book, is corroborated by flat headcount alongside rising contribution margin.

**What they have not delivered: growth, on any timetable they named.** The 12–16% contract-value target of May 2025 was never reached, never formally withdrawn, and quietly substituted. "A clear path back to double-digit growth" has now been asserted on four consecutive calls without arriving. Most damagingly, on 3 February 2026 the company beat the fourth-quarter estimate on both revenue and earnings and then guided 2026 below consensus, and the stock fell 31% in a day. A management team that beats the quarter and misses the year has, by definition, been managing the quarter.

**The sandbagging pattern is real and it is a two-edged instrument.** Safian is explicit about the method: "our philosophy generally is not build forecasts, plans and outlooks based on what we hope is going to happen, but more along what we've seen." Setting a beatable bar produces the perfect quarterly beat record. It also means the beats carry no information, which is exactly what the market concluded on 3 February.

**Third-party corroboration of the concern.** A securities class action, *Schmidt v. Gartner, Inc.*, is pending in the US District Court for the District of Connecticut on behalf of purchasers between 4 February 2025 and 2 February 2026; the deadline to apply as lead plaintiff was 18 May 2026. The published allegations are that Gartner "was not equipped to handle ongoing challenges in its industry to meet consulting revenue targets or to maintain its CV growth rate" and that executives "minimized slowdown risks." A separate strand, publicised from 11 February 2026, concerns the presentation of non-standard financial measures — which is the same issue as the September 2025 quarter's near-sixfold gap between adjusted and reported earnings. A lawsuit is an allegation, not a finding. But an independent party, with money at stake, has reached the same conclusion this section reached from the transcripts alone.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The question management answers but does not settle: is a large language model a substitute for a Gartner subscription?** It is asked, in some form, on three of the five calls. Jason Haas of Wells Fargo, August 2025: "what percentage of folks are citing usage of like a publicly available large language model and therefore, not consuming the Gartner subscription." Hall: "it's not material. It's basically -- it's essentially unmeasurable." Ashish Sabadra of RBC, November 2025, asks it again; Hall answers with intensified emphasis — "that comes up a very, very, very small number of transactions." The answer is internally consistent, it rests on a real tracking system (Gartner records a reason for every loss), and it has not changed across a year. It is also, necessarily, unauditable from outside. Management cannot prove a negative, and the market has decided not to take their word for it. This single unresolved question is the whole valuation argument.

**The topic analysts pushed on that later became bad news: consulting.** In May 2025 consulting was presented as strength — revenue up 5%, contract optimization up 38%, backlog up 16%. By February 2026 Reuters led its earnings story with "slowing demand at consulting unit," and the class action names the consulting outlook specifically. Analysts probed the durability of that backlog; management deflected toward its complementarity with research.

**The number management keeps explaining away: client count.** Jeff Silber of BMO in August 2025 — "the number of client enterprises... has been going down at least in GTS for the past couple of years, and now we're seeing it in GBS." Jasper Bibb of Truist asks the same in November. Both times the answer is identical: small technology vendors churning. It is a plausible and probably true explanation. It is also the fourth or fifth consecutive quarter of the same answer to the same question, and Safian's own November 2025 concession is the honest version: to reach 12–16% growth "we certainly need significant contribution from new logos as well."

**What analysts worry about that management does not address:** the arithmetic of an eight-to-ten-percent annual reduction in share count against roughly flat revenue. No one on any of the five calls asks what happens to the company when the buyback has consumed the balance-sheet capacity and revenue is still growing at one percent. Book equity is already down to $63 million.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Buying back stock at roughly $250, partly with borrowed money, while calling the programme "price sensitive"** (claim Q1 2025; execution Q3–Q4 2025; bond disclosed Q4 2025 call). The most concrete governance failure in the file.

🔴 **A near-sixfold gap between adjusted and reported earnings in the September 2025 quarter** ($2.76 vs $0.47) that the "ahead of expectations" framing passed over, and which now sits inside an active regulatory-disclosure investigation.

🔴 **A growth target announced, missed, and replaced without ever being formally retracted** (12–16% contract value, May 2025 → "double-digit," August 2025 → "over the medium term," November 2025 → 12% earnings per share, May 2026).

🔴 **Beating the quarter and guiding the year down** (3 February 2026, −31% in a session), which is the classic signature of short-horizon expectation management.

🔴 **Client enterprise count falling for multiple consecutive quarters** while revenue per client rises — a franchise harvesting its installed base rather than expanding it.

🟢 **Margins and cash actually improved through the worst of it.** Contribution margin 69% → 72% between September 2025 and March 2026; free cash flow up 29% year over year in the March 2026 quarter; profit and cash guidance raised twice during the downturn.

🟢 **Retention is turning before revenue does.** "Client retention rates are up about 100 bps year-over-year" (Q4 2025); wallet retention ticked up in Q1 2026; contract value growth stopped falling and rose from 0.8% to 1%. In a subscription business, retention leads revenue by a year — this is the first genuinely encouraging datum in the sequence.

🟢 **A real, testable product answer to the artificial-intelligence question.** AskGartner was rolled out to 100% of licensed users by October 2025 at no additional charge, and by February 2026 management could state that users of it "had substantially higher renewal rates than those who did not even with the same levels of engagement."

🟢 **Portfolio discipline.** The Digital Markets businesses — Capterra, Software Advice and GetApp — were agreed for sale to G2 on 29 January 2026, removing the piece of the portfolio most directly exposed to being replaced by a chatbot. Two new directors were added in January 2026, including Professor Daniela Rus of MIT, an artificial-intelligence and robotics specialist — a governance response aimed squarely at the bear case.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The rename is the tell.** Calling the segment "Business and Technology Insights" instead of "Research" is not cosmetic. "Research" is a category a language model can plausibly claim to compete in; "insights" is positioned as proprietary and relational. Management is repositioning the product away from the thing the market fears is being commoditised.

**"Journeys" has quietly become the load-bearing word.** By Q1 2026 the pitch is that clients' priorities "tend to be long, complex journeys," and Gartner guides them "at every stage." That is an argument for a relationship, not for a document library — again, a defence against substitution, encoded in vocabulary rather than argued directly.

**The proprietary-data recitation grows more insistent each quarter.** From "our 2,500 experts" and "500,000 one-on-one conversations" (Q1 2025), to "several hundred terabytes of highly proprietary data" (Q2 2025), to an itemised inventory of Key Metrics, 139,000 peer-network users and three million vendor ratings (Q3 2025). Management is constructing, in public, the case for why their input data cannot be scraped.

**A telling capability disclosure.** Q3 2025: "The amount of content published per analyst is up 31% year-over-year" and average publishing time is down 75%. Gartner is using generative artificial intelligence to raise the output of its own analysts by roughly a third. If the technology genuinely commoditised this work, it would first show up as the incumbent's own costs falling — which is precisely what is happening. That is an underweighted piece of evidence, and it cuts against the bear case.

**Sales-force mix shift.** Q4 2025 and Q1 2026: hiring is tilting from account managers (who defend existing revenue) toward business developers (who win new logos), because "business developer productivity has been actually quite strong." Territories per account manager are rising. This is a company that has concluded its existing client base cannot carry the growth.

**The one voice that changed.** Hall's closing remarks in Q1 2026 include "our teams are incredibly optimistic about our future" and a reference to spending time with "hundreds of our most successful salespeople." Appeals to internal morale in a closing statement are a soft signal that the external evidence is not yet doing the work.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: pivoting.** This is not a company gently deteriorating, and it is not one that has stabilised. It is mid-reconstruction: the core product organisation has been re-engineered along four declared dimensions, the flagship segment has been renamed, an artificial-intelligence delivery layer has been shipped to the whole client base, the most substitutable business line has been sold, the sales force is being re-weighted toward new-logo hunting, and the board has added artificial-intelligence expertise. Contract value growth has stopped falling and has begun, marginally, to rise. Whether the pivot works is unresolved; that a genuine pivot is under way is not in doubt.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** management has now promised a return to double-digit growth on four consecutive calls and has not delivered it once, while delivering flawlessly on every profit and cash-flow commitment it made. Size this position to the profit and cash record, not to the growth promise. Concretely: underwrite Gartner at roughly today's earnings power, treat any reacceleration as free optionality, and require the 4 August 2026 contract-value disclosure to confirm the Q1 up-tick before adding. The stock has fallen 27.6% in a day (5 August 2025) and 31% in a day (3 February 2026) on two of its last four reports; whatever the position size, it must survive a third such day.

**Economic moat: wide, with the edges being trimmed.** The moat is intangible-brand plus switching-cost, and it is unusually verifiable from outside the filings. The Magic Quadrant is not an information product but a *certification* in a two-sided market — buyers use it to justify decisions and vendors advertise placement in it, which is why fifteen-plus vendor press releases touting Gartner placements crossed the wire in the eight weeks to 27 July 2026. A language model can reproduce analysis; it cannot confer a badge that a procurement committee will accept. The returns evidence supports width rather than erosion: gross margin stable at 67.7%, contribution margin *rising* from 69% to 72% over the last two reported quarters, management's rolling four-quarter return on invested capital about 27% (the screener's fiscal-2025 figure is 21%), a 3.5% list-price increase pushed through with — in Hall's words — not "a lot of pushback," and client retention up about 100 basis points year over year. Returns and margins are not falling.

**Moat trend: eroding at the perimeter.** What *is* falling is reach. The client enterprise count has declined for several consecutive quarters, contract value growth has gone from 7% to roughly 1%, and the company now sells to 14,000 of an addressable 140,000 enterprises with the shrinking end of that base churning fastest. A franchise that can raise price but cannot add customers is compounding more slowly than it looks and is one demand shock away from compounding not at all.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural force is generative-artificial-intelligence displacement of knowledge work — the thesis that a language model makes syndicated research free. The evidence that it is *not* terminal is specific: Gartner's own loss-code tracking, a real system covering "the reason for every loss," has recorded language-model substitution as an immaterial cancellation reason for four consecutive quarters; users of Gartner's own artificial-intelligence tool renew at higher rates than non-users at equal engagement; the certification franchise is structurally unreplicable by a model; and the technology is currently *lowering* Gartner's cost to produce (31% more output per analyst). The evidence that it is not nothing: the customer count is genuinely shrinking, and management's reassurance is unfalsifiable from outside. The right reading is that the cheapness is mostly a fear-print on a durable franchise rather than a value trap on a melting base — but that reading is a judgement about an unresolved question, not a proven fact, and it must be sized as such.

bull_thesis:
Gartner sells subscription research and advice to senior executives, and it is priced today as though that business is being dismantled by artificial intelligence. The numbers say something different. At $150.41 a share the whole company is worth about $10.1 billion of equity and, adding its $1.69 billion of net debt, about $11.8 billion of enterprise value. Against that, the business threw off $1.26 billion of free cash flow in the last twelve months. That is roughly eight times cash earnings for a franchise whose gross margin is a stable 67.7%, whose contribution margin (revenue less the direct cost of serving a client) actually rose from 69% in the September 2025 quarter to 72% in the March 2026 quarter, and whose return on invested capital management put at about 27% on a rolling four-quarter basis on the May 2026 call. Businesses being destroyed do not expand their delivery margins while they are being destroyed.

The Magic Quadrant is a two-sided market: buyers use it to justify a purchase and vendors advertise their placement in it. In the eight weeks to 27 July 2026 at least fifteen separate technology companies -- Elastic, Grafana, Commvault, Arista, Coveo, SoundHound and others -- issued press releases announcing their Gartner placements. Management tracks a reason code for every single lost renewal, and asked directly on both the August and November 2025 calls how often clients cite a public language model as the substitute, Gene Hall's answer has not changed: 'it is not material... essentially unmeasurable.' Tellingly, the technology is currently cutting Gartner's own costs -- output per analyst is up 31% year over year and average publishing time is down 75%.

The second leg is that the leading indicators have already turned. In a subscription business, retention moves about a year before revenue does. Client retention was up roughly 100 basis points year over year as of the February 2026 call; wallet retention ticked up in the March 2026 quarter; contract value growth stopped falling and rose from 0.8% to 1%; free cash flow in that quarter was up 29%; and profit, earnings and cash-flow guidance were all raised. Management has also shipped a real product answer -- AskGartner went to 100% of licensed users at no extra charge by October 2025, and by February 2026 the company could state that users of it renewed at substantially higher rates than non-users at equal engagement levels. The most substitutable asset, the Digital Markets software-review sites, was agreed for sale to G2 on 29 January 2026 and is already out of the reported numbers.

The third leg is the share count. Trailing free cash flow of $1.26 billion against a $10.1 billion market value means Gartner can retire roughly a tenth of its own shares every year out of internally generated cash. Diluted shares have already gone from 78.0 million in the December 2024 quarter to about 67 million today. Consensus has adjusted earnings per share at $13.69 for 2026 and $15.38 for 2027 -- meaning the stock trades at about eleven times this year and under ten times next year for a business with a 24% profit margin and no meaningful growth required to get there.

Second, the client enterprise count -- which has fallen for several consecutive quarters -- must stabilise; management concedes that reaching its long-run target requires new logos, not just price. A target that is missed, never formally withdrawn, and quietly replaced four times in five quarters is not guidance; it is narrative maintenance. Consensus revenue for 2026 is $6.43 billion against $6.50 billion delivered in 2025. The top line is going backwards.

Underneath, the customer base is eroding at the edges. The number of client enterprises has fallen for several consecutive quarters. Management's explanation -- small technology vendors churning -- has been given in identical form to four different analysts across four calls, and it may well be true, but Craig Safian's own November 2025 concession is the operative one: to get back to the 12-16% range 'we certainly need significant contribution from new logos as well.' Gartner sells to 14,000 of an addressable 140,000 enterprises and the shrinking end of that base is churning fastest.

The consulting line is a live impairment, not a worry. It was presented as strength in May 2025 (revenue up 5%, contract optimisation up 38%, backlog up 16%). By 3 February 2026 Reuters led its story on the results with 'slowing demand at consulting unit,' and the pending securities class action names the consulting outlook specifically.

The governance record is the part that should give a buyer real pause. Gartner spent about $2.0 billion repurchasing its own stock in 2025 and a further $535 million in the March 2026 quarter -- roughly $2.5 billion in five quarters, about a quarter of today's entire market value. The largest tranche, $1.056 billion, was spent in the quarter ended September 2025, when the shares traded between roughly $226 and $352. That money is worth about 40% less today. Worse, on the February 2026 call management listed among its shareholder-friendly actions 'increasing leverage with a successful inaugural investment-grade bond offering to support even more share repurchase capacity' -- $525 million of net new debt in the December 2025 quarter, borrowed to buy stock at around $250 that now trades at $150. All of this while Gene Hall described the programme in May 2025 as 'price sensitive, opportunistic, and disciplined.' Book equity is now $63 million and net debt is $1.69 billion.

The accounting deserves scrutiny too. In the September 2025 quarter Gartner reported adjusted earnings of $2.76 a share against $0.47 under standard accounting rules -- a roughly $256 million non-cash charge stepped around by the adjusted figure, and the arithmetic reason full-year 2025 earnings per share fell 40% while every release said results were 'ahead of expectations.' A securities class action is pending in the District of Connecticut covering purchasers between 4 February 2025 and 2 February 2026, alleging that executives minimised slowdown risks and inflated the consulting outlook; a parallel strand concerns the presentation of non-standard financial measures.

Finally, the tape. This stock fell 27.6% in a single session on 5 August 2025 and 31% in a single session on 3 February 2026 -- on two of its last four reports. In the second case it beat the quarter on both revenue and earnings and guided the year below consensus. A company that beats the quarter and misses the year has been managing the quarter. Whoever owns this into 4 August 2026 is underwriting a third such day.

What would confirm the bear case: contract value growth at or below zero on 4 August; a further decline in client enterprise count; consulting revenue down year over year; or the securities case surviving a motion to dismiss and moving into discovery with a reserve that competes with the buyback.
consensus_delta:
The market is pricing terminal decline into a business whose earnings power is stable and whose delivery margins are still expanding. That is the disagreement, and it is worth being precise about which street assumptions are wrong and which are right.

Wrong: the assumption that generative artificial intelligence is already substituting for Gartner subscriptions. The published street work leans on this -- the 5 February 2026 sell-side note that reiterated a hold cited 'AI disruption fears persist' alongside the contract-value slowdown, treating the two as one phenomenon. The company's own disclosure separates them. Gartner records a reason code for every lost renewal, and asked twice by name -- Jason Haas of Wells Fargo in August 2025 and Ashish Sabadra of RBC in November 2025 -- what share of cancellations cite a public language model, Gene Hall's answer was 'it is not material... essentially unmeasurable' and then 'a very, very, very small number of transactions.' What management does describe, repeatedly and specifically, is budget behaviour: 'my CFO says cut half expenses,' seats not backfilled when an executive retires, approval authority escalating from the function head to the chief financial officer. Those are cyclical mechanics, not substitution. The strongest single piece of counter-evidence is that the technology is currently making Gartner cheaper to run -- output per analyst up 31% year over year, publishing time down 75%. A force that commoditises an incumbent does not first show up as the incumbent's own costs falling.

Also wrong: the implicit assumption that the Magic Quadrant is an information product. It is a certification in a two-sided market. In the eight weeks to 27 July 2026, at least fifteen technology vendors issued press releases advertising their Gartner placements. A language model can write the analysis; it cannot issue a badge a procurement committee will accept.

Right, and this is where we do not disagree with the street: the growth is genuinely stalled, the client enterprise count is genuinely falling, consulting is genuinely impaired, and management has genuinely forfeited the right to be believed on the reacceleration timetable. The 12-16% contract-value target set in May 2025 was missed, never withdrawn, and quietly replaced three times. The February 2026 session, when Gartner beat the quarter on both lines and guided the year below consensus and fell 31%, was the market correctly repricing a management team that had been managing the quarter.

The net expectations gap is therefore narrower than the headline discount suggests, and it is a gap about *duration*, not about *level*. The market is paying eight times trailing free cash flow for a franchise whose cash flow is not falling. Our base case of $185 is about seven percent above the highest recent street target of $183 and roughly seven percent above the consensus of $173. That is a real but modest disagreement -- and after a twelve-percent two-day run it is no longer a wide enough one to act on today.
forcing_function:
There are two, operating on very different clocks.

The near one is the second-quarter 2026 report on 4 August 2026, and specifically the contract value growth rate disclosed with it. That single number is the referendum on whether the last eighteen months were a technology-budget freeze or the beginning of structural substitution, and it is the only piece of evidence either side can point to that the other cannot dismiss. Management staked itself to it on 5 May 2026: 'Looking ahead to the rest of the year, we expect contract value will accelerate.' Two consecutive quarters of acceleration -- 0.8% to 1% to something visibly higher -- would break the value-trap framing and force the multiple to move, because at eight times trailing free cash flow the market is currently paying nothing for growth of any kind. A flat or negative print does the reverse, just as fast.

The slower and more reliable one is the share count. Gartner generated $1.26 billion of free cash flow over the last twelve months against a $10.1 billion equity value. Diluted shares have already fallen from 78.0 million in the December 2024 quarter to about 67 million today, a reduction of roughly fourteen percent, and the company spent $535 million on repurchases in the March 2026 quarter alone. If the business simply holds its current earnings power, retiring nine or ten percent of the shares a year compounds earnings per share at that rate with no operational improvement required at all. This is why the company retargeted its public promise in May 2026 to 'adjusted EPS on a compound annual basis above 12% over the next 3 years' -- it is the one number the buyback can deliver unaided. It is a slow forcing function, but it does not depend on management being believed.

What is deliberately not counted as a forcing function: the Digital Markets sale to G2 (agreed 29 January 2026, already in the reported numbers) and the securities litigation (undated, multi-year). Neither creates near-term asymmetry.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next three to nine months, and it has three distinct parts.

First, and most immediately, 4 August 2026. Consensus is $3.77 in adjusted earnings on $1.648 billion of revenue, but the earnings line is not the risk -- Gartner has beaten the earnings estimate in all seven of its last seven quarters and the beats now carry almost no information. The risk is the contract value growth rate. If it prints at or below the 1% of the March quarter, the last statistical support for 'cyclical, not structural' disappears and the twelve-month low of $124.25 is back in play immediately. If it prints negative, the adverse case of $112 becomes the working assumption rather than the tail. This name has fallen 27.6% and 31% in single sessions on two of its last four reports; a third such day is an ordinary outcome, not a stress scenario. Timing is one small mercy: the current market regime read flags the 22-30 July window as the densest event cluster of the year (the Federal Reserve meeting on 28-29 July, the large-cap technology capital-spending guides on 29-30 July, June inflation data and second-quarter output on 30 July) and notes that events landing inside that cluster risk muted or delayed re-rates while early-August landings are cleaner. Gartner reports just after it, so the print should get an undistracted audience.

Second, the legal overhang, which is undated and therefore cannot be waited out. Schmidt v. Gartner is pending in the District of Connecticut; the lead-plaintiff deadline passed on 18 May 2026, which means the case now moves to a consolidated complaint and a motion to dismiss. A dismissal removes an overhang. A survived motion means years of discovery, a settlement reserve, and -- more corrosively -- a management team distracted precisely while it is trying to re-engineer its core product. The parallel strand concerning the presentation of non-standard financial measures is the more uncomfortable one, because the September 2025 quarter's near-sixfold gap between adjusted earnings of $2.76 and reported earnings of $0.47 is a matter of record, not allegation.

Third, the macro and financing setting. Rate-cut relief is not coming: the policy rate sits at 3.50-3.75% and a hike by December is the priced base case, so a thesis that leans on cheaper money is dead on arrival -- and this one does not lean on it, which is a point in its favour. But Gartner now carries $2.98 billion of borrowings against $63 million of book equity, with quarterly interest expense of about $21 million and rising, having levered up specifically to fund buybacks at roughly $250 a share. That removes the balance-sheet cushion that would otherwise let the company buy aggressively into its own dislocation. Broader positioning is also unhelpful: fund-manager cash at 3.6% is at a level historically read as a sell signal, and in that configuration negative surprises travel considerably farther than positive ones.

There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall. Free cash flow is $1.26 billion a year and cash on hand is $1.67 billion. The risk here is entirely to the multiple, not to solvency.
positioning_washout:
The forced-selling phase is largely complete, which is the strongest structural argument for owning this eventually -- but it is emphatically not happening this week, which is the argument for not owning it today.

The handoff from growth ownership to value ownership has already run. The stock is down about 58% from its twelve-month high of $357.33 and touched $124.25 along the way. Growth mandates have been exiting on the record: the Virtus SGA Global Growth Fund disclosed in its first-quarter 2026 update that it had exited its Gartner position outright. On the other side, the name now screens as value -- Zacks published 'Here's Why Gartner is a Strong Value Stock' twice in six weeks, on 15 June and 6 July 2026. Sell-side coverage has thinned and de-rated in the same direction: twenty-eight price targets over the past year averaged $209, but only seven in the last quarter averaged $162, and only one has been published in the last month. That is what a shareholder base changing hands looks like, and most of the mechanical work has been done.

There is no dividend to cut, so there is no income-fund liquidation to come. There is no index-deletion risk of consequence at a $10 billion market value. And there is a large, price-insensitive buyer permanently in the market: at roughly $500 million a quarter of repurchases against a $10.1 billion equity value, Gartner is absorbing a meaningful share of its own float every quarter.

But the tape right now is the opposite of washed out. The shares have gone from $133.69 on 23 July to $150.41 today, up about twelve percent in two sessions, on no company-specific news that a licensed news search can identify. It is a group move -- Forrester was up 4.8% and Information Services Group up 1.8% in the same session -- which reads as a sentiment bid on the research and advisory complex rather than anything Gartner-specific. Buying an eight-day-out binary into a two-day squeeze is the wrong end of the trade. The washout to wait for is a disappointing contract-value print that takes the stock back toward the $124-130 area on heavy volume; that is where the forced-selling argument and the valuation argument finally point the same way.
moderator_conclusion:
This committee covered Gartner recently and concluded to wait for the wash-out rather than buy. Nothing dated has happened to the business since -- no earnings, no guidance change, no legal development -- so that call is carried forward unchanged. What has changed is the price, and it has moved against the buyer: the shares have run from about $139 when we last looked to $150.41 today, including a twelve-percent jump over two sessions on no company-specific news, alongside a broad rally in the research and advisory group. A rising price with an unchanged fair value is a smaller margin of safety, not a better one, so if anything the case for patience is stronger than it was.

The underlying judgement is unchanged and worth restating plainly. This is a genuinely high-quality franchise on sale. Gartner earns a 67.7% gross margin, converts 18% of revenue into free cash, and expanded its delivery margin from 69% to 72% over the last two reported quarters while the market decided its business model was obsolete. The moat is a wide and unusually verifiable one -- the Magic Quadrant is a certification in a two-sided market, which is why fifteen-plus technology vendors publicised their placements in the last eight weeks, and a language model cannot issue a badge a procurement committee will accept. The multiple, at eleven times this year's earnings and eight times trailing free cash flow, is priced for a melting base that the delivery margins say is not melting. Our base-case value by parts is $185 a share, against $150.41 today.

But the discount is not large enough to overcome three things. First, the moat is being trimmed at the perimeter: the client enterprise count has fallen for several consecutive quarters, contract value growth has gone from 7% to roughly 1%, and a franchise that can raise price but cannot add customers compounds far more slowly than it looks. Second, the forensic record is not clean. Management promised a return to 12-16% growth in May 2025, missed it, never withdrew it, and quietly replaced it three times -- ending in May 2026 with an earnings-per-share target that a buyback can deliver regardless of what the business does. Worse, having called its repurchase programme 'price sensitive, opportunistic, and disciplined,' the company spent $1.056 billion in the September 2025 quarter at a tape averaging roughly $250, and then borrowed $525 million more in the December quarter to keep buying -- while the stock went to $150. That is a real governance mark, and an independent party with money at stake has reached a similar conclusion: a securities class action is pending in the District of Connecticut, with a parallel strand concerning the September 2025 quarter's near-sixfold gap between adjusted and reported earnings. Third, and decisively for timing, the report on 4 August is eight days away, and this stock has fallen 27.6% and 31% in single sessions on two of its last four reports.

On the catalyst itself, the house rule is that a scheduled event is descriptive, not a scoring lever -- we do not add conviction for event heat any more than we deduct it for a spent one. So the 4 August print is not why this is a three. The three is the residual value case: about a quarter of upside to a fair value we hold with real but bounded confidence, roughly a quarter of downside to an adverse case that the market has already visited this year, a wide moat whose reach is narrowing, and a management team we trust completely on cash and not at all on growth. Judged with the catalyst overlay stripped out entirely, the value case scores the same three -- the valuation is attractive but not exceptional after the bounce, and the forensic record is the specific thing holding it back from more.

The regime read reinforces the patience. Rate-cut rescue is off the table with a December hike still the priced base case, and this thesis does not need one, which is to its credit. But two features cut against acting now: positioning is full, with fund-manager cash at a level historically read as a sell signal, meaning negative surprises travel farther than positive ones; and the resolution driver here -- whether generative artificial intelligence displaces knowledge work -- is the single most crowded shared macro question in this market and the one the book is most concentrated in. Sizing discipline requires treating that as correlated risk, not idiosyncratic edge.

The level to wait for is specific: a disappointing contract-value figure on 4 August that returns the shares to the $124-130 area on heavy volume. That is where the forced-selling argument and the valuation argument finally point in the same direction, and where the margin of safety would be wide enough to absorb being wrong about the artificial-intelligence question. Alternatively, and less likely, a visibly accelerating contract-value print would break the value-trap framing outright and justify paying up -- but that is a decision to make with the number in hand, not eight days before it.

interrogator_dossier:
# Gartner, Inc. (NYSE: IT) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Five consecutive quarterly calls, May 2025 through May 2026, cross-checked against the reported financials, the price tape, and the litigation record. Price used throughout: $150.41 (NYSE, US dollars, live quote 27 July 2026). Gartner sells subscription research and advice to senior executives; its single most important operating number is contract value, the annualised dollar amount of research subscriptions on its books at a point in time.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across five calls the story does not change its facts so much as it steadily relocates the finish line.

**May 2025 (first quarter 2025).** The tone is one of confident endurance. Contract value grew 7%. Gene Hall, the chairman and chief executive, frames a hard environment as temporary and enumerates the shocks the company has already survived — "the COVID-19 pandemic, the bursting of a tech spending bubble, the highest inflation in 40 years." The forward promise is specific and quantified: "We expect to reaccelerate CV growth to our target of 12% to 16%, when the macroeconomic environment returns to normal." Blame is assigned to two identifiable, containable buckets: the US federal government (about 4% of contract value, hit by the Department of Government Efficiency) and tariffs.

**August 2025 (second quarter).** The narrative pivots hard, and this is the most important shift in the whole sequence. Hall opens by naming two takeaways, and the first is artificial intelligence: "AI is an important opportunity for Gartner across several dimensions." The second is an admission dressed as a plan — "we're making adaptations that give us a clear path back to double-digit growth." Note the quiet demotion: in May the target was 12–16%; by August the aspiration is "double-digit." The company also renames its largest segment from Research to Business and Technology Insights, and launches AskGartner, an artificial-intelligence assistant that has "been in development for almost 2 years." A new headwind is introduced: "Measures of CEO confidence fell to recessionary levels, among the fastest drops ever recorded."

**November 2025 (third quarter).** Contract value growth is 3%, less than half the level of two quarters earlier. The emphasis moves decisively from growth to proof-of-engagement metrics and to capital returns: "we repurchased more than $1 billion of stock in the quarter, reducing share count by 6% year-over-year." The reacceleration language softens again, now qualified by time: a "clear path back to long-term sustained double-digit growth **over the medium term**."

**February 2026 (fourth quarter).** This is the capitulation call, and the market treated it as one — the stock fell 31% in a single session. Hall abandons the "the environment will normalise" frame entirely and replaces it with a structural self-criticism: "driving incremental improvements on our standard practices wasn't enough. To achieve step change improvements, we needed to rethink many of our processes and practices." The transformation is formalised along four dimensions — impact, volume, timeliness, user experience. Crucially, the payoff window is pushed out again: "We believe this transformation will provide a step change in the value to our clients **over the next few years**." A definitive agreement to sell the Digital Markets business is disclosed alongside.

**May 2026 (first quarter 2026).** A modest, genuine stabilisation. Contract value grew 1% — an acceleration, from a very low base. Free cash flow rose 29% year over year. Guidance for profit, earnings and cash flow was raised. And the growth promise is restated one more time, in yet another new form: "we expect to deliver adjusted EPS on a compound annual basis above 12% over the next 3 years." Observe what has happened over five calls: the 12–16% *contract value* target of May 2025 has become a 12% *earnings per share* target — and earnings per share is the one line a large buyback can deliver regardless of what the business does.

**Quietly dropped along the way:** the phrase "return to historically strong productivity"; the specific 12–16% contract-value target; and the framing that the headwinds are federal-government and tariff-specific. **Quietly added:** artificial intelligence as both the top client demand topic and the company's own product story; share-count reduction as the headline shareholder-value mechanism.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where and when | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We expect to reaccelerate CV growth to our target of 12% to 16%" | Hall, Q1 2025 | Contract value growth went 7% (Q1 2025) → 3% (Q3 2025) → 0.8% (Q4 2025) → 1% (Q1 2026). The target was never approached; it was silently replaced. | **Contradicted** |
| "a clear path back to double-digit growth" | Hall, Q2 2025 | Repeated in some form on every subsequent call. Two quarters after it was first said, growth hit 0.8%. Consensus revenue for 2026 is $6.43B against $6.50B delivered in 2025 — a *decline*. | **Contradicted** |
| Financial results "ahead of expectations" | Every one of the five calls | True, and consistently so. Reported earnings per share beat the consensus estimate in all seven of the last seven quarters: $2.50 vs $2.37, $2.98 vs $2.72, $3.53 vs $3.30, $2.76 vs $2.43, $3.94 vs $3.50, $3.32 vs $2.99. | **Corroborated** |
| Margins and cash generation are holding | Safian, Q3 2025 and Q1 2026 | Genuinely strong. Total contribution margin (revenue less the direct cost of delivering it) rose from 69% in Q3 2025 to 72% in Q1 2026. Gross margin is a stable 67.7%. First-quarter 2026 free cash flow was $371M, up 29%. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $1.26B on $6.5B of revenue — an 18% free-cash-flow margin. | **Corroborated** |
| "we generate free cash flow well in excess of net income" | Hall, repeatedly | Correct and materially so: $1.26B of trailing free cash flow against roughly $741M of trailing net income, a ratio of about 1.7x, because subscriptions are billed in advance. | **Corroborated** |
| Pricing power is intact; "we do not offer discounts" | Safian, Q1 2026; Hall, Q3 2025 on the 3.5% list increase | Supported by the margin evidence above and by rising wallet retention. Also supported by a fact outside the filings: in the eight weeks to 27 July 2026 at least fifteen separate technology vendors issued press releases advertising their placement in a Gartner Magic Quadrant. Vendors do not pay to publicise a badge that has stopped mattering. | **Corroborated** |
| Buybacks are executed "by being price sensitive, opportunistic, and disciplined" | Hall, Q1 2025 | This is the single worst-supported claim in the file. See below. | **Contradicted, severely** |

### The buyback, priced against the tape

Gartner repurchased about $2.0 billion of its own stock during 2025 (cash-flow statement: $163M, $274M, $1,056M and $498M by quarter) and a further $535M in the first quarter of 2026 — roughly $2.5 billion in five quarters, equal to about a quarter of today's entire $10.1 billion market value.

The largest single tranche, $1.056 billion, was spent in the quarter ended September 2025. Gartner shares closed at $352.47 on 28 July 2025, $336.71 on 4 August 2025, and traded between roughly $226 and $265 for the balance of that quarter. A reasonable average execution price for that tranche is around $250. The stock is $150.41 today. That one quarter's repurchase is worth roughly 40% less than what was paid for it — on the order of $400 million of value transferred from continuing holders to exiting ones.

It gets harder to defend. On the February 2026 call Hall listed among 2025's "shareholder value-enhancing actions" both the $2 billion of buybacks and "increasing leverage with a successful inaugural investment-grade bond offering to support even more share repurchase capacity." The cash-flow statement confirms $525M of net debt issuance in the fourth quarter of 2025. Gartner borrowed money to buy its own shares at roughly $250 while telling investors the programme was price-sensitive. Net debt now stands at $1.69 billion (borrowings of $2.98B plus $372M of capitalised leases, less $1.67B of cash) against a balance sheet whose book equity has been reduced to $63 million.

To be fair to the other side of the ledger: at today's $150 the same programme is genuinely powerful. Trailing free cash flow of $1.26 billion against a $10.1 billion market value means Gartner can retire something like a tenth of its own shares every year without borrowing a dollar. The criticism is of the execution, not the instrument.

### The gap between reported and adjusted profit

In the quarter ended September 2025, Gartner reported adjusted earnings of $2.76 per share. Reported earnings under standard accounting rules were $0.47 per share — a factor of nearly six. The cash-flow statement shows a $256 million non-cash item added back that quarter, and reported operating income collapsed to $86 million from a roughly $330 million quarterly run-rate. That single quarter is the arithmetic reason the full-year 2025 earnings per share of $9.65 was down 40% year over year while every quarterly press release said results were "ahead of expectations." Investors reading only the adjusted line would not have registered it.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: declining, then stabilising at a lower level.**

- *Q1 2025 — offensive.* "We'll target our investments to support long-term sustained double-digit growth." Headcount in sales grew 4%. The company is investing into the downturn.
- *Q2 2025 — first defensive turn.* The vocabulary changes to adaptation and containment: "we're making adaptations," "we're expanding our capabilities," and, on costs, "we're prepared to tighten the belt maybe one more notch if we have to." Safian confirms sales headcount will "end the year roughly flattish."
- *Q3 2025 — proof-seeking.* Growth metrics are replaced by leading indicators of growth: "Client engagement was up in the quarter," "our new business pipeline is up double digits," "Attendee ratings of our conferences are reaching all-time highs." When a company substitutes engagement statistics for revenue statistics, it is telling you the revenue statistics are not ready.
- *Q4 2025 — defensive and self-critical.* "Executives have responded to this by slowing and deferring everything possible. This makes for a much tougher selling environment." Then the striking planning assumption from the analyst session: "we're certainly assuming that this year 2026, that the selling environment is going to be no better anticipated in 2025... we're assuming behind is not going to get better at all." That is prudent, and it is also the first time in the sequence that management has stopped forecasting a recovery in demand.
- *Q1 2026 — cautiously constructive.* "New business with enterprise leaders was strong in the first 2 months of the quarter. Due to changes in the geopolitical environment, client decisions slowed somewhat in March." Note the precision — they are now dating the slowdown to a specific month, which is a more falsifiable and therefore more credible form of disclosure than the sweeping macro narratives of a year earlier.

On specificity, the record actually improves. Early calls offered a sweeping numeric target with no delivery. Recent calls offer narrower, checkable claims — "the number of high-impact documents [is up] 22%," "the number of documents in our insights library is up 19%," "we've reduced our average publishing time by 75% compared to last year," "licensed users who use AskGartner had substantially higher renewal rates than those who did not even with the same levels of engagement." These are testable. Management has traded the grand promise for the modest measurable, which is usually what a management team does when it has been burned — and it is a mild positive for credibility going forward.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: low-to-medium.** The split is unusually clean and worth stating precisely, because the two halves point in opposite directions.

**What they have delivered, without exception: profit, margin and cash.** Seven consecutive quarterly earnings beats. Guidance for profit, earnings and free cash flow was *raised* in both November 2025 and May 2026, in the middle of the worst demand stretch in a decade. Free cash flow of $1.26 billion over the last twelve months exceeds net income by about 70%. Management controls costs with real skill — Safian's description of "territory optimization," reallocating sales coverage away from the shrinking federal book, is corroborated by flat headcount alongside rising contribution margin.

**What they have not delivered: growth, on any timetable they named.** The 12–16% contract-value target of May 2025 was never reached, never formally withdrawn, and quietly substituted. "A clear path back to double-digit growth" has now been asserted on four consecutive calls without arriving. Most damagingly, on 3 February 2026 the company beat the fourth-quarter estimate on both revenue and earnings and then guided 2026 below consensus, and the stock fell 31% in a day. A management team that beats the quarter and misses the year has, by definition, been managing the quarter.

**The sandbagging pattern is real and it is a two-edged instrument.** Safian is explicit about the method: "our philosophy generally is not build forecasts, plans and outlooks based on what we hope is going to happen, but more along what we've seen." Setting a beatable bar produces the perfect quarterly beat record. It also means the beats carry no information, which is exactly what the market concluded on 3 February.

**Third-party corroboration of the concern.** A securities class action, *Schmidt v. Gartner, Inc.*, is pending in the US District Court for the District of Connecticut on behalf of purchasers between 4 February 2025 and 2 February 2026; the deadline to apply as lead plaintiff was 18 May 2026. The published allegations are that Gartner "was not equipped to handle ongoing challenges in its industry to meet consulting revenue targets or to maintain its CV growth rate" and that executives "minimized slowdown risks." A separate strand, publicised from 11 February 2026, concerns the presentation of non-standard financial measures — which is the same issue as the September 2025 quarter's near-sixfold gap between adjusted and reported earnings. A lawsuit is an allegation, not a finding. But an independent party, with money at stake, has reached the same conclusion this section reached from the transcripts alone.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The question management answers but does not settle: is a large language model a substitute for a Gartner subscription?** It is asked, in some form, on three of the five calls. Jason Haas of Wells Fargo, August 2025: "what percentage of folks are citing usage of like a publicly available large language model and therefore, not consuming the Gartner subscription." Hall: "it's not material. It's basically -- it's essentially unmeasurable." Ashish Sabadra of RBC, November 2025, asks it again; Hall answers with intensified emphasis — "that comes up a very, very, very small number of transactions." The answer is internally consistent, it rests on a real tracking system (Gartner records a reason for every loss), and it has not changed across a year. It is also, necessarily, unauditable from outside. Management cannot prove a negative, and the market has decided not to take their word for it. This single unresolved question is the whole valuation argument.

**The topic analysts pushed on that later became bad news: consulting.** In May 2025 consulting was presented as strength — revenue up 5%, contract optimization up 38%, backlog up 16%. By February 2026 Reuters led its earnings story with "slowing demand at consulting unit," and the class action names the consulting outlook specifically. Analysts probed the durability of that backlog; management deflected toward its complementarity with research.

**The number management keeps explaining away: client count.** Jeff Silber of BMO in August 2025 — "the number of client enterprises... has been going down at least in GTS for the past couple of years, and now we're seeing it in GBS." Jasper Bibb of Truist asks the same in November. Both times the answer is identical: small technology vendors churning. It is a plausible and probably true explanation. It is also the fourth or fifth consecutive quarter of the same answer to the same question, and Safian's own November 2025 concession is the honest version: to reach 12–16% growth "we certainly need significant contribution from new logos as well."

**What analysts worry about that management does not address:** the arithmetic of an eight-to-ten-percent annual reduction in share count against roughly flat revenue. No one on any of the five calls asks what happens to the company when the buyback has consumed the balance-sheet capacity and revenue is still growing at one percent. Book equity is already down to $63 million.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Buying back stock at roughly $250, partly with borrowed money, while calling the programme "price sensitive"** (claim Q1 2025; execution Q3–Q4 2025; bond disclosed Q4 2025 call). The most concrete governance failure in the file.

🔴 **A near-sixfold gap between adjusted and reported earnings in the September 2025 quarter** ($2.76 vs $0.47) that the "ahead of expectations" framing passed over, and which now sits inside an active regulatory-disclosure investigation.

🔴 **A growth target announced, missed, and replaced without ever being formally retracted** (12–16% contract value, May 2025 → "double-digit," August 2025 → "over the medium term," November 2025 → 12% earnings per share, May 2026).

🔴 **Beating the quarter and guiding the year down** (3 February 2026, −31% in a session), which is the classic signature of short-horizon expectation management.

🔴 **Client enterprise count falling for multiple consecutive quarters** while revenue per client rises — a franchise harvesting its installed base rather than expanding it.

🟢 **Margins and cash actually improved through the worst of it.** Contribution margin 69% → 72% between September 2025 and March 2026; free cash flow up 29% year over year in the March 2026 quarter; profit and cash guidance raised twice during the downturn.

🟢 **Retention is turning before revenue does.** "Client retention rates are up about 100 bps year-over-year" (Q4 2025); wallet retention ticked up in Q1 2026; contract value growth stopped falling and rose from 0.8% to 1%. In a subscription business, retention leads revenue by a year — this is the first genuinely encouraging datum in the sequence.

🟢 **A real, testable product answer to the artificial-intelligence question.** AskGartner was rolled out to 100% of licensed users by October 2025 at no additional charge, and by February 2026 management could state that users of it "had substantially higher renewal rates than those who did not even with the same levels of engagement."

🟢 **Portfolio discipline.** The Digital Markets businesses — Capterra, Software Advice and GetApp — were agreed for sale to G2 on 29 January 2026, removing the piece of the portfolio most directly exposed to being replaced by a chatbot. Two new directors were added in January 2026, including Professor Daniela Rus of MIT, an artificial-intelligence and robotics specialist — a governance response aimed squarely at the bear case.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The rename is the tell.** Calling the segment "Business and Technology Insights" instead of "Research" is not cosmetic. "Research" is a category a language model can plausibly claim to compete in; "insights" is positioned as proprietary and relational. Management is repositioning the product away from the thing the market fears is being commoditised.

**"Journeys" has quietly become the load-bearing word.** By Q1 2026 the pitch is that clients' priorities "tend to be long, complex journeys," and Gartner guides them "at every stage." That is an argument for a relationship, not for a document library — again, a defence against substitution, encoded in vocabulary rather than argued directly.

**The proprietary-data recitation grows more insistent each quarter.** From "our 2,500 experts" and "500,000 one-on-one conversations" (Q1 2025), to "several hundred terabytes of highly proprietary data" (Q2 2025), to an itemised inventory of Key Metrics, 139,000 peer-network users and three million vendor ratings (Q3 2025). Management is constructing, in public, the case for why their input data cannot be scraped.

**A telling capability disclosure.** Q3 2025: "The amount of content published per analyst is up 31% year-over-year" and average publishing time is down 75%. Gartner is using generative artificial intelligence to raise the output of its own analysts by roughly a third. If the technology genuinely commoditised this work, it would first show up as the incumbent's own costs falling — which is precisely what is happening. That is an underweighted piece of evidence, and it cuts against the bear case.

**Sales-force mix shift.** Q4 2025 and Q1 2026: hiring is tilting from account managers (who defend existing revenue) toward business developers (who win new logos), because "business developer productivity has been actually quite strong." Territories per account manager are rising. This is a company that has concluded its existing client base cannot carry the growth.

**The one voice that changed.** Hall's closing remarks in Q1 2026 include "our teams are incredibly optimistic about our future" and a reference to spending time with "hundreds of our most successful salespeople." Appeals to internal morale in a closing statement are a soft signal that the external evidence is not yet doing the work.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: pivoting.** This is not a company gently deteriorating, and it is not one that has stabilised. It is mid-reconstruction: the core product organisation has been re-engineered along four declared dimensions, the flagship segment has been renamed, an artificial-intelligence delivery layer has been shipped to the whole client base, the most substitutable business line has been sold, the sales force is being re-weighted toward new-logo hunting, and the board has added artificial-intelligence expertise. Contract value growth has stopped falling and has begun, marginally, to rise. Whether the pivot works is unresolved; that a genuine pivot is under way is not in doubt.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** management has now promised a return to double-digit growth on four consecutive calls and has not delivered it once, while delivering flawlessly on every profit and cash-flow commitment it made. Size this position to the profit and cash record, not to the growth promise. Concretely: underwrite Gartner at roughly today's earnings power, treat any reacceleration as free optionality, and require the 4 August 2026 contract-value disclosure to confirm the Q1 up-tick before adding. The stock has fallen 27.6% in a day (5 August 2025) and 31% in a day (3 February 2026) on two of its last four reports; whatever the position size, it must survive a third such day.

**Economic moat: wide, with the edges being trimmed.** The moat is intangible-brand plus switching-cost, and it is unusually verifiable from outside the filings. The Magic Quadrant is not an information product but a *certification* in a two-sided market — buyers use it to justify decisions and vendors advertise placement in it, which is why fifteen-plus vendor press releases touting Gartner placements crossed the wire in the eight weeks to 27 July 2026. A language model can reproduce analysis; it cannot confer a badge that a procurement committee will accept. The returns evidence supports width rather than erosion: gross margin stable at 67.7%, contribution margin *rising* from 69% to 72% over the last two reported quarters, management's rolling four-quarter return on invested capital about 27% (the screener's fiscal-2025 figure is 21%), a 3.5% list-price increase pushed through with — in Hall's words — not "a lot of pushback," and client retention up about 100 basis points year over year. Returns and margins are not falling.

**Moat trend: eroding at the perimeter.** What *is* falling is reach. The client enterprise count has declined for several consecutive quarters, contract value growth has gone from 7% to roughly 1%, and the company now sells to 14,000 of an addressable 140,000 enterprises with the shrinking end of that base churning fastest. A franchise that can raise price but cannot add customers is compounding more slowly than it looks and is one demand shock away from compounding not at all.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural force is generative-artificial-intelligence displacement of knowledge work — the thesis that a language model makes syndicated research free. The evidence that it is *not* terminal is specific: Gartner's own loss-code tracking, a real system covering "the reason for every loss," has recorded language-model substitution as an immaterial cancellation reason for four consecutive quarters; users of Gartner's own artificial-intelligence tool renew at higher rates than non-users at equal engagement; the certification franchise is structurally unreplicable by a model; and the technology is currently *lowering* Gartner's cost to produce (31% more output per analyst). The evidence that it is not nothing: the customer count is genuinely shrinking, and management's reassurance is unfalsifiable from outside. The right reading is that the cheapness is mostly a fear-print on a durable franchise rather than a value trap on a melting base — but that reading is a judgement about an unresolved question, not a proven fact, and it must be sized as such.
